title: Input Range, PSRR, Noise and Offset
intro: The accuracy floor of an op amp: how far its input common-mode level can move, how well it rejects supply noise, how much noise and offset it adds (Razavi, Sections 9.8, 9.11 and 9.12).

blocks.text: Differential input swings are tiny (the output divided by the open-loop gain), but the input common-mode level may have to travel, as in a unity-gain buffer where the input follows the output. There the input pair, not the output stage, limits swing: $V_{in,min} \approx V_{GS1,2} + V_{ISS}$, about a threshold above what the output devices allow. Below it the tail source enters triode, the tail current and $g_m$ fall, and the amplifier degrades.

The standard fix is complementary input pairs: an NMOS and a PMOS pair in parallel, each feeding a folded cascode. Near ground the NMOS pair dies but the PMOS pair works, and near $V_{DD}$ the reverse. The total transconductance then varies with input CM, roughly doubling in the middle, so gain, speed and noise vary too; more elaborate circuits hold the total $g_m$ constant.

blocks.alt: Plot of transconductance against input common-mode level from 0 to VDD. The PMOS pair's gm is constant at low levels and falls to zero near VDD; the NMOS pair's is zero near ground and rises to constant. Their sum is g near both rails and 2g in the middle.
blocks.caption: Complementary input pairs keep the stage alive from rail to rail, but the total $g_m$ is not constant.

blocks.text: A mismatch between the two halves produces an output with zero differential input; referred to the input it is a random part of a few millivolts plus any systematic part (for example unequal drain voltages in a mirror load). The random part of a pair scales roughly as $1/\sqrt{WL}$, so large input devices reduce it, at the price of capacitance. Offset and its drift are treated in the chapter on nonlinearity and mismatch.

PSRR is a ratio of two gains: how strongly the input reaches the output, over how strongly $V_{DD}$ does. In a five-transistor OTA with a current-mirror load, the diode-connected PMOS clamps its gate to $V_{DD}$ minus a nearly constant $V_{GS}$; by symmetry the output follows the same way, so the gain from $V_{DD}$ to the output is close to one and

Closing a feedback loop around the op amp lowers the supply gain and the input gain by the same factor, $1 + $ loop gain, so it does not improve PSRR. At high frequencies capacitances couple the supply to internal nodes and PSRR degrades; fully differential circuits help because supply noise appears as a common-mode disturbance.

A quick way to find the noise contributors: imagine wiggling each transistor's gate and ask whether the output moves. Cascode devices barely matter at low frequency (their noise current mostly circulates through themselves), leaving the input pair and the current-source loads.

items: Telescopic: $M_1$-$M_2$ and the PMOS sources $M_7$-$M_8$. Thermal part $\overline{V_n^2} = 8kT\gamma\left(\frac{1}{g_{m1,2}} + \frac{g_{m7,8}}{g_{m1,2}^2}\right)$, flicker part $\frac{2K_N}{(WL)_{1,2}C_{ox}f} + \frac{2K_P}{(WL)_{7,8}C_{ox}f}\frac{g_{m7,8}^2}{g_{m1,2}^2}$.

Folded cascode: the input pair plus two sets of current sources, the PMOS loads $M_7$-$M_8$ and the folding sources $M_9$-$M_{10}$, all of which move the output. $\overline{V_n^2} = 8kT\gamma\left(\frac{1}{g_{m1,2}} + \frac{g_{m7,8} + g_{m9,10}}{g_{m1,2}^2}\right)$. So it is noisier than a telescopic op amp; for low flicker noise use a PMOS input pair.

Two-stage: the second stage's noise is divided by the first stage's gain when referred to the input, $\overline{V_n^2}\big|_{M5-8} = \frac{8kT\gamma(g_{m5} + g_{m7})}{g_{m1}^2(r_{O1} \parallel r_{O3})^2g_{m5}^2}$, usually negligible; the first stage dominates.

blocks.text: Current sources contribute in proportion to their $g_m$, so swing and noise trade: lowering a source's overdrive to free headroom raises $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OD}$ and its noise. Power and noise also trade through linear scaling: halving all widths and currents halves power and doubles $\overline{V_n^2}$, with gain and swing unchanged.

These specifications together set the resolution of a signal chain. A 12-bit converter's front end, for example, needs input noise well below one LSB and an offset that is either small next to one LSB or calibrated out.

blocks.title: Offset and area
blocks.text: A pair has a random offset of 4 mV for $WL = 10\;\mu\text{m}^2$. What area gives 1 mV?
solution: Offset scales as $1/\sqrt{WL}$. Cutting it by 4 requires 16 times the area: $160\;\mu\text{m}^2$.

blocks.title: Low-frequency PSRR
blocks.text: A five-transistor OTA has $g_{mN} = 1$ mS and $r_{ON} \parallel r_{OP} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$. Estimate its low-frequency PSRR.
solution: Supply gain $\approx 1$; differential gain $= 1\text{ mS} \times 50\text{ k}\Omega = 50$.

blocks.text: For the same input pair ($g_{m1} = 2$ mS) and PMOS loads ($g_{m7} = 1$ mS), a folded cascode adds folding sources with $g_{m9} = 2$ mS. By how much does its thermal noise power exceed the telescopic version's?
